column16:
At Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the Department of Aviation (DOA) has implemented a policy requiring contractors to divert at least 90% of C&D debris from landfill disposal. This includes recycling and reusing concrete, asphalt, metals, drywall, and wood, as well as prioritizing deconstruction techniques where feasible. Materials are either recycled on-site, sent to certified recycling facilities, or redirected for community reuse programs. The DOA's diversion program has become a national model for airports, demonstrating how large-scale capital projects can significantly reduce embodied carbon emissions and landfill dependency. Department of Aviation has set a target to divert 90 percent of all airport waste from landfills by 2035. This includes both operational waste and construction and demolition debris, with diversion tracked and required in all major capital projects. Since 2016, the airport has diverted more than 95,000 tons of C&D waste from landfill and achieved an average diversion rate of 87 percent.

The City also partners with local deconstruction and reuse organizations to extend the life cycle of salvaged building materials, integrating them into affordable housing and community development projects. Together, these measures position Atlanta as a leader in embedding circular economy principles into the construction sector while cutting carbon emissions associated with both material production and disposal.

ATL is committed to employing sustainable design and construction practices while maintaining operations as the world's busiest airport. ATL's Planning and Development (P&D) Sustainability Standards integrate industry best practices, aiming to reduce water use, energy consumption, and environmental impacts, including embodied carbon in building materials. ATL was the first airport to earn LEED for Communities certification and continues to pursue additional certifications across numerous projects and rating systems, including LEED, Parksmart, and Envision. Innovative practices and technologies, like the modular construction approach, carbon mineralization of concrete, and maturity meters that more accurately predict in-situ strength of concrete—reducing overall cement content and associated embodied carbon, further exemplifying ATL's commitment.

column16: In his London Environment Strategy (LES) the Mayor set a target to reduce food waste by 20% per head by 2025 and by 50 % per head by 2030, and to send zero biodegradable waste to landfill by 2026, in line with emerging Sustainable Development Goal 12.3 reduction targets, and signed up as '12.3 Champion'. Achieving this target will lead to a significant reduction in the core materials associated with food packaging: paper, card, plastic, glass, tins and cans, which collectively make up around 75 per cent of municipal waste.https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/london_environment_strategy_0.pdf. The Mayor of London also published the London Food Strategy in 2018 that aims to ensure a Londoners have access to healthy and sustainable food.https://www.london.gov.uk/sites/default/files/final_london_food_strategy.pdf. The Mayor entered into a partnership with ReLondon and the Ellen MacArthur Foundation in 2019 to deliver against his LES targets, the Food Flagship Initiative (FFI). Through the FFI the Mayor together with ReLondon and London Councils commissioned research exploring the way material flows through the entire food and beverage supply chain within Greater London: from production, to imports, to consumption, to how waste is managed. Following the publication of the report - London's Food Footprint - the Mayor committed to: convening a food supply roundtable with representatives of the food sector with the largest impact to reduce consumption emissions from the supply chain; producing a pathway to the achieving the food waste reduction targets set out in the LES; and leading by example by using the purchasing power of the GLA and wider GLA group to measure and reduce food waste and consumption-based emissions of supply chains, working with suppliers, including catering contractors to achieve this. https://relondon.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/ReLondon_Londons_food_footprint_online.pdfhttps://relondon.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/London-food-commitment-2021.pdf. The Mayor has delivered against all three commitments. London's Food Supply Chain Roundtable was held in September 2023 with 35 of the largest businesses from across the food system attending and committing to work with the city to accelerate food waste reduction. The GLA' Group Responsible Procurement Policy and Implementation Plans were published in August 2022, providing guidelines for reducing emissions through the GLA's purchasing activities. The Mayor commissioned the Waste & Resources Action Programme to produce London's Food Waste Reduction Pathway outlining actions to take to release his LES targets. This report will be published in August 2024. ReLondon identified the reduction of consumption-based emissions of CO2e as a focus of its Business Plan 2020 -25. ReLondon also identified five focus areas in its Circular Economy Route Map: food, plastics, electronics and electrical equipment, textiles and the built environment. ReLondon continues to fund activities that can reduce waste and increase recycling in these five areas and accelerate a transition to a circular economy. They place an emphasis on activities relating to municipal waste, and in particular food. Food is both a significant contributor to London's consumption-based emissions, and a large component of the municipal waste stream.https://relondon.gov.uk/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/LWARB-Business-Plan-FINAL.pdf . ReLondon are continuing to deliver projects to reduce food waste and transition to a circular food system, through a pan-London awareness raising campaign Eat Like A Londoner, researching barriers to efficient food redistribution and creating a circular food neighbourhood with Islington Council.

column16: The London Environment Strategy has a commitment to monitor and report on London's scope 3 emissions. This includes construction emissions. The London Plan 2021 requires all strategic developments to calculate and reduce whole life-cycle carbon emissions (including embodied carbon from construction), using GLA benchmarks to enable performance comparison and report on actual embodied carbon reductions achieved post-construction. This provides an estimation of the carbon emissions resulting from the materials, construction and the use of a building over its entire life, including its demolition and disposal. A WLC assessment provides a true picture of a building's carbon impact on the environment. Guidance and a reporting template to support this process has been developed setting out the detailed requirements: https://www.london.gov.uk/what-we-do/planning/implementing-london-plan/london-plan-guidance/whole-life-cycle-carbon-assessments-guidance. Additionally, the London's NRMM Low Emission Zone uses the Mayor and London Borough's planning powers to control emissions from NRMM used on construction sites. To date, the policy has delivered a significant improvement in emissions from construction site equipment, equivalent to an annual reduction of 42 per cent PM, 36 per cent NOX and 11 per cent CO2, when compared to a 2019 base year. The standards become progressively tighter over time, and by 2040 only zero emission NRMM will be permissible at all construction sites in London. Full details of current and future standards can be found on the website, https://www.london.gov.uk/what-we-do/environment/pollution-and-air-quality/nrmm

BFC has been hosting sustainable fashion shows since 2010 to showcase designers who work sustainably. The BFC launched the Institute of Positive Fashion in recognition of the urgent challenge of climate change. In September 2017, in partnership with Vivienne Westwood and the BFC, the Mayor launched the “Fashion SWITCH to Green” initiative which signed up major brands which were committed to switching to a green energy supplier by 2020.The BFC is also taking the lead in setting standards for equality and diversity. It is currently convening meetings to create workstreams, including working conditions, diverse representation, and education and careers to drive change. Last year, BFC partnered with BBC Earth to highlight the environmental impact of the fashion industry and promote more mindful consumer decisions. Also ReLondon through its work with policy-makers, business and citizens, has in the last two years: contributed to Environment Audit Committee's 'Fixing Fashion' report; worked with fashion brands and retailers to help them roll out new circular business models; campaigned as #LoveNotLandfill to raise awareness of clothing waste amongst London's 16-24 year olds; and is working with London Councils One World Living Programme, Ellen MacArthur Foundation to develop an action plan to reduce textiles waste and transition to a circular textiles economy. In June 2023 ReLondon published London's Fashion Footprint a material flow analysis mapping the flow of materials across the textiles industry, the associated emissions and identifying levers for climate action. In response to the report the Mayor committed to bringing together industry to explore opportunities to promote circular businesses models across the supply chain; through the Love Not Landfill and Repair Week campaigns engage with partners to expand activities targeting fast fashion and reduce volumes of consumption; and convene London's boroughs to explore opportunities to lead by example, using their purchasing power to measure and reduce the emissions associated with the clothing they and their partners purchase.

Oslo has an Action plan for sustainable, healthy and more plant-based food in the City of Oslo:
Byrådssak - Handlingsplan for bærekraftig, sunn og mer plantebasert mat i Oslo kommune

The main objective of the action plan is that the City of Oslo's food consumption contributes to good public health and animal welfare, while indirect greenhouse gas emissions and negative impacts on the environment and society is significantly reduced. The action plan has four sub-goals:

• Sub-goal 1: The City of Oslo has halved its meat consumption and increased the proportion of plant-based food by year 2025 with the year 2019 as a starting point (to be revised)
• Sub-goal 2: The City of Oslo has increased its expertise in sustainable, healthy and good plant-based food 
• Sub-goal 3: The City of Oslo has halved its food waste by 2030 with the year 2019 as starting point
• Sub-goal 4: The City of Oslo has contributed to developing the supplier market for sustainable food and emphasizes animal welfare and working conditions through the procurement and consumption of food and drink

Reporting on the measures outlined in the action plan happens biannually, but a selection of the most significant measures is also included in the table of measures to reduce indirect emissions in the Climate Budget, and is reported on three times yearly. This keeps track of the meat consumption (kilos) and vegetarian food as a standard for all meetings and events hosted by the municipality.

The City Council's goals for a circular Oslo: 
a) Consumption of virgin natural resources has been reduced to a level that can be considered compatible with global sustainable consumption. At the same time, we have achieved: b) Increased local employment in value chains based on circular resource use. c) Increased circular innovation and value creation. 

A coordinated approach across sectors is a prerequisite for success in the transition to a circular economy. The thematic plan is therefore cross-sectoral and shows how the municipality will work to promote a more circular economy in Oslo. 

The thematic plan emphasizes four areas with particularly great potential for circular solutions. The four areas are consumption and retail trade, building and construction, resources from waste and the innovation district in Hovinbyen as a test arena for circular economy.

The agency for climate coordinates the efforts to achieve the goals of the thematic plan, and is currently working on including circular economy in the City's climate budget process.

60% actual recycling of household-like waste The target of annual 60% actual recycling is measured based on the amount of resources sorted by Copenhagen residents that are ultimately recycled at treatment facilities. It also includes waste from public institutions and business located in residential buildings using the public system.
30,000 tons of commercial waste for recycling The target is to collect 30,000 tons of commercial waste in 2030. Recycling of commercial waste in Copenhagen is measured as the amount of waste sorted by businesses in the city as a result of municipal inspections and guidance provided on proper waste management.
60,000 tons of construction and demolition waste for recycling The target of diverting 60,000 tons of construction and demolition waste from incineration to recycling is measured as a cumulative figure over the entire planning period. Cool Food Pledge

As part of the TransformTO Net Zero Strategy, City Council directed the Director, Environment and Climate, in coordination with Executive Director, Social Development, Finance and Administration and the Chief Procurement Officer, Purchasing and Materials Management, to identify ways that the City can support the reduction of the greenhouse gas emissions associated with food the City of Toronto procures, in alignment with the City's Cool Food Pledge and the C40 Good Food Cities Declaration, 
and to report back in the second quarter of 2023 on the status of corporate and community food-related emissions and recommended actions for the TransformTO 2026-2030 short-term action plan, including a goal to maximize local, organic and fair trade food procurement.

As part of the C40 Good Food Cities Declaration, Cities will implement the following measures by 2030:
- Aligning our food procurement to the Planetary Health Diet, ideally sourced from organic agriculture.
- Supporting an overall increase of healthy plant-based food consumption in our cities by shifting away from unsustainable, unhealthy diets.
- Reducing food loss and waste by 50 per cent from a 2015 baseline.
- Within two years of endorsing this declaration, working with citizens, businesses, public institutions and other organizations to develop a joint strategy for implementing these measures and achieving these goals inclusively and equitably, and incorporating this strategy into our Climate Action Plan.

Latest update on Toronto's Coolfood Pledge available at: https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2024/ie/bgrd/backgroundfile-246860.pdf


About Toronto's Local Food Procurement Policy

The City's Local Food Procurement Policy endeavours to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions associated with the provision of food purchased for City operations and facilities while supporting local producers and processors. All RFPs and RFQs to purchase food for City of Toronto operations (greater than $3,000) include language indicating that it is a policy objective of the City to increase the percentage of food that is grown locally when all factors, including costs, quality and availability are equal.

Policy available at: https://secure.toronto.ca/council/agenda-item.do?item=2011.GM5.13


About the Good Food Cities Declaration:

At the C40 world Mayors Summit on October 9-12, 2019, in Copenhagen, Denmark, the Mayor of Toronto signed the Good Food Cities Declaration, along with a number of mayors from cities across the world. The declaration is a commitment by cities to achieve a 'Planetary Health Diet' for all citizens by 2030 by: 

a) Shifting Food Procurement; 
b) Increasing healthy plant-based food Consumption; and 
c) Reducing Food Loss and Waste.

Toronto's City Council directed the City Manager to report in the second quarter of 2020 with a plan and timelines for the City of Toronto to implement the short-term and long-term goals of the 2015 Milan Urban Food Policy Pact, to which the City is a Signatory City, and the C40 Good Food Cities Declaration, which was signed by Mayor John Tory on October 10, 2019 in Copenhagen, Denmark, including those pertaining to food procurement, consumption, and food loss and waste.

City Council also committed to achieving the World Resources Institute's Cool Food Pledge to reduce the greenhouse gas emissions associated with the food the City of Toronto procures by 25 percent by 2030 relative to 2015 and City Council request the City Manager to report in the second quarter of 2020 on a plan and timelines to implement the goals of the Pledge.

As part of the Long Term Waste Management Strategy, the City of Toronto is working towards an aspirational goal of zero waste and a circular economy. To drive innovation and the growth of a circular economy in Toronto, the City established a Circular Economy and Innovation unit within the Solid Waste Management Services Division, 
making it one of the first municipalities in North America to form a dedicated circular 
economy team. 

A circular economy aims to reduce waste and maximize resources by moving away from the linear take-make-and-dispose approach to an innovative system that focuses on product longevity, renewability, reuse and repair. Circular economy strategies consider resource consumption and material efficiency for their potential impacts on climate change, environmental degradation, and social outcomes. Cities are well-positioned to play a critical role in achieving climate neutrality and moving to more sustainable consumption models. 

To advance more circular and sustainable consumption and achieve its waste reduction goals, the City of Toronto is developing a Circular Economy Road Map that will help guide Toronto to becoming the first municipality in the province with a circular economy. Work on the Road Map began in 2020 with the launch of the Baselining for a Circular Toronto Study. The project involved a city-wide landscape analysis, examining the economic, environmental, social and policy conditions related to a circular economy; three sector-specific material flow analyses, examining resource use and disposal in waste, construction, and the food system; and a 'business as usual' analysis of the resource consumption and waste generation by these sectors in 2030, if left unchanged. This study also identified visions and goals for the City of Toronto's circular economy 
transition, which will form the launching point for the development of the Circular Economy Road Map. 

Once finalized, Toronto's Circular Economy Road Map will inform policy and program changes to advance the City's aspirational circular economy goals.

column16: The city of Athens follows the national legislation towards the reduction of municipal waste and the National Plan of Waste Management and is very active on the transformation of waste management into a circular one. The plan describes measures and initiatives to prevent waste generation, promote re-use, increase recycling rates, promote the market for secondary materials, inform and raise awareness among citizens, rapidly develop bio-waste and recyclable material collection networks, create modern facilities for waste and bio-waste management and the utilisation of waste fuels. Among the objectives included in the plan are landfill targets of less than 10% in the year 2030 (5 years earlier than corresponding European provisions) and reduction of biological and degradable waste (paper and organic) sent to landfills to 35% (by weight) compared to the production levels of the specific waste in 1997. The quantitative targets defined at the national level also concern Athens. Although they have not been fully legislated, they can be a point of reference for the Municipality's goals for recycling and reducing the amount of waste and processing it in landfills.

En junio de 2024, la Ciudad de México publicó a través de la Gaceta Oficial, el “Aviso por el cual se da a conocer el Programa de Certificación Cero Residuos de Alimentos de la Ciudad de México”, dicho programa tiene como objetivo, reducir el desperdicio de alimentos y evitar la generación de residuos orgánicos que comúnmente son enviados a sitios de disposición final como rellenos sanitarios. 

Este programa se alinea estrechamente con las metas del Programa de Gestión Integral de Residuos de la Ciudad de México (PGIR 2021-2025) y del Plan de Acción Basura Cero, con lo que se se busca contribuir a la reducción de emisiones de CyGEI.

Este Programa está formulado para que los grandes generadores de residuos puedan diseñar y ejecutar un Plan de implementación Cero Residuos de Alimentos durante un periodo de 18 meses. El plan se conforma por una serie de criterios voluntarios que tienen por objetivo prevenir y reducir el desperdicio de alimentos hasta en un 50 por ciento.

Aunado a lo anterior, la Ciudad de México cuenta con proyectos relacionados a la disminución de emisiones por medio del tratamiento de alimentos: 
-Laboratorio de producción de biodiésel en Central de Abastos: consiste en una planta de biodiésel de la Central de Abasto (CEDA) que permitirá convertir el aceite comestible residual en un combustible ecológico vegetal y del que se producirán tres mil litros diarios.

-Mercado de Trueque: es un programa de educación ambiental, enfocado en la separación de residuos sólidos domiciliarios desde el origen, y en la promoción del reciclaje para la conservación de los recursos naturales y la biodiversidad, así como para la mitigación del cambio climático, en la Ciudad de México. El programa consiste en el intercambio entre los residuos sólidos reciclables limpios y ordenados, por artículos de primera necesidad, plantas, hortalizas y/o servicios, que son incentivos para motivar el interés y participación en el mejoramiento ambiental.

-Aprovechamiento por composta de los residuos orgánicos y de poda: Como parte de las acciones que realiza la Ciudad de México, existe un programa en donde una parte de los residuos orgánicos que se producen en la ciudad se reutilizan para generar composta y evitar que éstos sigan emitiendo metano a la atmósfera.

El programa 'Reciclatrón' promueve entre la ciudadanía el correcto manejo, separación y reciclaje de residuos electrónicos y eléctricos, los cuales son recibidos en este programa y se enlistan con base en la Norma Ambiental para el Distrito Federal NADF-019-AMBT-2018, Anexo I).

Los residuos electrónicos y eléctricos requieren un plan de manejo especial para acopiarlos, transportarlos y aprovechar su valor o gestionar su disposición final de manera ambientalmente adecuada y controlada. Su principal acción es realizar jornadas de acopio en donde la ciudadanía lleva sus aparatos electrónicos para su reciclaje y correcta disposición en vez de que estos terminen en tiraderos. 

Durante 2022, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente, capacitó a las Alcaldías de la Ciudad de México para que realicen de manera independiente sus propias jornadas de reciclatrón.

Con la puesta en marcha de éste programa de educación ambiental contribuimos de manera directa a la reducción de residuos a través del acopio de éstos para su reciclaje. 

El Reciclatrón ofrece a la población la posibilidad de acudir a jornadas participativas a entregar sus residuos y recibir, a cambio, diversas clases de bienes generados por productoras y productores locales, entre otros.

Desde que inició este programa, hasta julio de 2025, se han realizado 164 jornadas, se han recolectado 2,450 toneladas de este tipo de residuos electrónicos, lo que representa un avance significativo en el manejo responsable de los mismos. Además, han participado más de 108,000 personas que han contribuido al reciclaje adecuado de aparatos eléctricos y electrónicos.

The Paris Climate Action Plan aims to support a sustainable and quality food and to decrease by 40% the carbon footprint of the territory related to the food industry. It also sets objectives for the sector in terms of carbon impact of food. These are declined and focused on within the Paris Strategy for Sustainable Food (Stratégie de Paris pour une Alimentation Durable 2018-2030) focusing on the whole territory, and to a lesser extent, the Sustainable Food Plan (Plan Alimentation Durable 2022-2027), which concerns City run restauration.

The Paris Food Strategy has a strong ambition to respond concretely to the ecological, economic and food challenges of today: to develop a sustainable food system that is inclusive, resilient, safe and diversified, and to promote access to healthy, local and affordable food for all, resilient, safe and diversified, and to promote access to healthy, local and affordable food for all. 

By 2030, it notably aims :
- to reach 50% of food consumed coming from the Parisian Basin (25% in 2017).
- to reach 20% of agriculture surfaces to be certified organic within the Ile-de-France region (2,7% in 2017) 
- reduce local meat consumption and obesity rates (with the target of 5% against 10,7% in 2017).

In line with the Sustainable Food Plan, the 'Parisculteurs' program, gastronomic innovation, plans to combat food waste, waste recovery and support for businesses and waste or the support for food shops and markets and food markets implemented by Paris, the Food strategy provides the city with an ambitious, cross-cutting food policy at the territorial level.

The council of Paris adopted in late 2024, its new Local Waste Prevention Plan (PLPDMA), taking into account the trajectory set by the Climate Action Plan regarding reduction of waste related emissions. 

This new plan set a clear target, reducing produced waste by 20% by 2030 compared to the 2010 baseline (French law requires -15%). As such, this represents reaching a reduction of 100 000 tons annual over the course of the Plan, which is a target of 830 000 tons of waste instead of the 930 000 tons observed in 2023.

Accompanying this structural objective, the PLPDMA aims to reach an overall valorization rate of 60% by 2030, which amounts to ambitious captation rates for each types of waste (75% for plastic an paper, against 29% in 2023, 50% for foodwaste against 1%, 75% for glass against 61% and 80% for occasional bulk waste against 60%).

Behind these targets, the plan set 24 effective actions to consume better, sort at home, reduce professional waste, as well as generalize foodwaste sorting, street waste sorting, better construction and make the City administration an example. A Plastic Free Olympics - during the summer of 2024 the City succeeded in hosting a plastic free Olympics offering visitors and Parisians an experience without single use plastics for beverages food and residual goodies. The goal was to promote bulk shopping and reuse on a larger scale in daily life spaces. Reduction and reuse were the main drivers to achieve a plastic free experience in celebration zones and around official sites such as the Seine riverbanks experimental areas and tourist landmarks. Zero 

Plastic Ambition for Parisians This ambition translates into concrete actions for Parisians including: 
(i) eliminating plastic in school canteens and childcare facilities, 
(ii) establishing a unique network of public water fountains to reduce the need for plastic bottles, 
(iii) developing a consignment system and supporting solution providers. Implementing an Eco responsible charter for events in Paris banning single use plastics. Introducing nudges in three Parisian sports centers, 
(iv) expanding the fountain network with an inclusive model called Mât Source 100 fountains by 2024, 
(v) ending all single use plastic purchases in Parisian markets. 

The 2024 Action Plan: while Paris strives to set an example, it acknowledges the need for collective efforts. After two conferences in 2019 and 2021 with over 400 participants the City organized the third annual conference on October, 5, 2022, to present the action plan and operations until 2024. An annual evaluation of the application of the plan in 2023 was outed in 2024 and showed notable advancement. This year, more than 1,300 municipal staff were trained in environmental issues and a network of 1,500 committed economic players was created.

The waste management strategy of Rotterdam firstly focusses on decreasing the amount of residual waste to work towards the circular economy in 2050. All materials will be separated and reused, preferably as high on the 'R-ladder' as is possible. We stimulate using products longer, not throwing consumption items away but repair, share, trade etc. to shrink down the amount of produced waste and to create awareness about the value of materials by our inhabitants.

•Processing waste streams locally is one of the criteria when creating new contracts with waste processors. Also route optimization for our collection trucks contributes to less emissions. 

•Creating a waste collection system for high rise buildings other than, by example, twenty containers along the street to collect the waste more compact means more efficiency and thus less collection trucks driving through the city centre. 

•The municipality lends cargo bikes to transport bigger waste objects towards waste collection points where the municipality recycles those materials. 

•We also contributed to a food waste challenge in which ten restaurants and hotels measured their food waste for half a year and received advice about reducing food waste. This way those ten restaurants and hotels prevented 36.292kg CO2 emission and 2.804kg food waste. The aim is to continue those challenges and that those excited entrepreneurs word of mouth spreads the attention about food waste throughout the city.

column16: In order to strengthen the effectiveness of Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) reviews and enhance environmental benefits, on October 24, 2016, the City issued and implemented the \'Taipei City Environmental Impact Assessment Criteria for Promoting a Livable and Sustainable City\', which requires that EIA development projects in the City should obtain a silver level or higher green building label and install photovoltaic power generation equipment. column16: The Green Cities Action Plan details the City's commitment to reduce its GHG emissions. The Action Plan was developed with support from the IFC. The strategy looks at four main sectors: waste, energy, built environment and transport , water and wastewater. GHG savings have been calculated for each sector from the City of Ekurhuleni's 2030 targets, and these have been linked to individual measures that would need to be implemented across the City. As an action plan, the document provides initial costing and potential funding sources for all prioritized actions. The waste characterization study that has been finalised takes the Green City Action plan further. C40 Cities is supporting the City in closing collection gaps, improving residual waste disposal solutions, phasing out organics from disposal, and creating and upskilling jobs. The project seeks to understand the waste composition and mass flow in the City, through conducting a waste characterization and quantification study within Ekurhuleni. The study seeks to provide valuable insights into the waste management practices of the City and help identify areas where improvements can be made to reduce waste generation, increase recycling, and minimize environmental impacts. By understanding the composition and mass flow of waste in Ekurhuleni, there may be a need to develop strategies and policies to promote more sustainable waste management practices. By reducing the disposal of food waste and improving waste operations and infrastructure, C40 Cities can lead a historical opportunity to make significant contributions to avoid the worst impacts of climate change for this generation and deliver local benefits to their communities.

This report documents the outcomes from research into clean construction in Ekurhuleni, South Africa. It is one of a series that forms part of the C40 Clean Construction Programme. Informed by evidence gathered from literature reviews and interviews with cross-sectoral public and private stakeholders, the report sets out an overview of the construction industry landscape in the city. It presents insights into the current state of construction and clean construction activities already adopted in the city as well as barriers and opportunities to implementing bolder and more ambitious actions. It then proposes a series of recommended clean construction measures the city could adopt, addressing whole life greenhouse gas emissions together with wider social, economic, and environmental issues.

El Plan Integral de Movilidad Urbana Sustentable (PIMUS), prevé la creación de Zonas de Bajas Emisiones (ZBE) en la metrópoli, también conocidas como Zonas de Aire Limpio, las cuales son áreas delimitadas en donde se implementen acciones para desincentivar el uso de vehículos contaminantes al consolidar la oferta de movilidad activa, transporte público limpio y la implementación gradual de controles de acceso, circulación y estacionamiento de vehículos automotor. Esta medida busca implementar estos polígonos en la metrópoli para mejorar la calidad del aire y reducir las emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero.

El Gobierno de Guadalajara junto con C40 Cities e Imeplan gestionaron el proyecto ”Estudio de
factibilidad para la implementación de una Zona de Bajas Emisiones (ZBE) en Guadalajara, México” que tuvo el objetivo de acompañar la implementación de acciones estratégicas del sector transporte derivadas del Plan de Acción Climática del Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara (PACmetro). Este consistió tanto en el diseño de una metodología para seleccionar áreas con potencial para implementar la acción, el diseño de medidas para iniciar y consolidar el proyecto, y la estimación de los beneficios de la implementación progresiva de la ZBE en el polígono definido.

- En enero del 2024 se inauguró la zona de bajas emisiones en Paseo Alcalde derivado del proyecto anteriormente mencionado. Actualmente se trabaja en el diseño de una estrategia para consolidar el proyecto, así como una guía para replicar y escalar en otros municipios de la metrópoli.

Se puede consultar más información en: https://www.c40.org/es/news/guadalajara-announces-mexicos-first-low-emission-zone/

Los Puntos Verdes Metropolitanos (PVM) son espacios donde se reciben, acopian, y envían los residuos para su valorización en una dinámica de economía circular, propiciando la conexión entre comunidad, naturaleza y territorio. Basados en el modelo de gestión de residuos del Área Metropolitana de Barcelona a través de su experiencia y apoyo técnico.

EL Área Metropolitana de Guadalajara cuenta con 9 PVM distribuidos y emplazados de manera estratégica en los municipios metropolitanos. En cada uno de ellos, se realiza recepción de residuos valorizables para su correcta disposición y actividades para concientizar sobre el consumo responsable.
Los PVM forman parte de la acción Metro Resilience Guadalajara (MRG) o Metrópoli Resiliente, por su adaptación al español, reúne esfuerzos comunitarios, locales e internacionales, para fortalecer la gobernanza con el fin de responder, adaptar y prosperar ante los desafíos urbanos en las Áreas Metropolitanas de Guadalajara (AMG) y Barcelona (AMB).
Es una acción de cooperación internacional con duración de 3 años (2022-2025), la cual es posible gracias al financiamiento de la Unión Europea y el programa Asociación para ciudades sostenibles.

column16: The City is addressing transportation emissions by encouraging the use of public transit and other non-car transportation and land use planning. The City of Mimi is integrated into the broader Miami Dade County transit system and falls under the auspices of the Miami-Dade Transportation Planning Organization (TPO). Miami-Dade County is currently making progress towards the implementation of the Strategic Miami Area Rapid Transit (SMART) plan and implemented a reorganization of its bus program and routes under the “Better Bus Network” plan. Miami-Dade's Better Bus Network launched in November 2023. Miami-Dade has made progress on the SMART plan through progressing to the implementation phase of its Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) corridor along US-1 linking South Dade to the metro-rail metro-mover network. As of February 2025, construction was at 92% complete which includes 14 BRT stations. The City offers numerous free public transit options including a Citywide free trolley system, the free Metromover in Downtown (operated by Miami-Dade County), and the Freebee. The free trolley system, with 13 routes, provides over 4 million rides annually, supplementing the County operated bus system. Freebee, a free electric vehicle shuttle service operates in several Miami neighborhoods (Coconut Grove and Brickell/Downtown). The program has expanded to include on demand rides from Tesla vehicles within defined service areas. In 2025, Circuit Transit, Inc was authorized to be used in the Coconut Grove neighborhood for free on-demand transportation services. Another key initiative is the expansion of electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure, including the installation of more EV charging stations throughout the city to support the transition to electric vehicles. Through the FPL EVolution program, the City will be installing 22 DC Fast/Level 3 charging ports across 6 City parks and 2 City parking lots. Additionally, the City promotes the use of shared micromobility options like Citi Bike and electric scooters to reduce reliance on single-occupancy vehicles. These efforts are complemented by investments in public transit improvements and the development of pedestrian-friendly infrastructure to encourage walking and cycling. In addition, the City completed an update of the Bicycle Master Plan in 2023 and is currently finalizing additional edits anticipated to be completed in 2025. The City has seen investment in high-quality bike/ped pathways with Miami-Dade County installing protected bike lanes in downtown Miami, the completion of Phase 2 of The Underline, and the City securing 60 million from U.S. DOT for the I-395 Graham Heritage Trail, to reconnect underserved communities that were displaced when the Interstate was built. However, the City was informed in August 2025 that funding has been rescinded by the federal government for the Graham Heritage Trail in accordance with “HR 1 One Big Beautiful Bill” therefore the project is on hold until new funding is secured. Likewise, the City Commission approved the Reimagine Parks Miami Master Plan in July 2023 which includes recommendations for development of additional high-quality bicycle and pedestrian connectors.

column16: While City of Miami's GHG inventory does not show waste to be a significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions since the City's waste is processed via waste-to-energy, we recognize the importance of addressing the waste stream. The City has included the following actions in its GHG reduction plan in an effort to address issues with the waste stream:•A-1: Improve city data on waste streams and disposal. Establish a per capita waste goal. •A-3: Implement green and sustainable special events program.•A-6: Improve recycling participation and reduce contamination.•A-7: Work with community composting organizations to increase household composting. In addition, the City partnered with the Ocean Conservancy and University of Georgia to develop a Circularity Assessment Protocol (CAP) to analyze sources of plastic pollution and develop recommendations to address and eliminate these pollutants. Developed by the Circularity Informatics Lab at the University of Georgia, the CAP is a standardized assessment protocol to inform decision-makers through collecting community-level data on plastic usage. Grounded in materials flow and systems thinking concepts, the CAP uses a hub-and-spoke model to holistically characterize how consumer plastic flows into a community, is consumed, and flows out, either through waste management systems or leakage into the environment. The model, shown below, is comprised of seven spokes: input, community, material and product design, use, collection, end of cycle, and leakage. At the center, the system is driven by policy, economics, and governance with key influencers including non-governmental organizations, industry, and government. The City of Miami offers single stream recycling to residents. Per Sec 22-19 of the City code, a multi-family residence of four units or more shall provide for a recycling program and shall include, at a minimum, the following five listed materials: (1)Mixed-paper, cardboard.(2)Glass (flint, emerald, amber).(3)Aluminum cans.(4)Steel cans.(5)Plastics, coded 1—7. Per Sec 22-20 of the City code, it shall be the responsibility of the owner, occupant, tenant, or lessee of the commercial establishment to properly dispose of all recyclable material generated by such commercial property. Every commercial property shall provide for a recycling program which shall include a minimum of three materials of its choice selected from the following list: (1)High grade office paper.(2)Mixed paper.(3)Corrugated cardboard.(4)Glass (flint, emerald, amber).(5)Aluminum (cans, scrap).(6)Steel (cans, scrap).(7)Other metals/scrap production materials.(8)Plastics (PETE, HDPE-natural, HDPE-colored).(9)Textiles.(10)Wood. It is considered a violation of the code to not provide a recycling program as laid out above.

Food Systems Programs Impact through implementation of the 2025 Food Action Plan (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/food/2025%20Phoenix%20Food%20Action%20Plan%20Jan%202020.pdf) serves as guidance on activities to provide healthy food for all in Phoenix through a resilient, sustainable, thriving, and equitable local food system with healthy, affordable, and culturally relevant food for all. The City's Food Systems Program achieved over 90% of the goals in the 2025 Food Action plan. From 2020 through 2025, the actions identified in the 2025 plan were achieved through the Phoenix Resilient Food Systems Initiative using municipal funds and American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds. The City innovatively and creatively used the funds available for food assistance by creating 14 programs. Through the collective efforts of our community partners, grantees, and Phoenix residents, we've made significant progress toward the goals outlined in the 2025 Phoenix Food Action Plan. The following summarizes the most notable outcomes of RFSI initiative: Meals Distributed: 5,546,605 meals were distributed to residents during and post-pandemic. Pounds of Food Produced Overall: 51,264 pounds of food were produced across 12 grant projects and the Backyard Garden Program. Grant Funds Distributed: $1,808,694 and 31 projects were supported between 2022 and 2024, which supported local farmers and non-profit organizations to increase food access and implement innovative practices, such as agrivoltaics, indoor vertical farming, portable cold storage containers, irrigation and shade improvements. Food Waste Diverted: 94,840 pounds (over 47 tons!) of food waste was diverted from landfills; Local Businesses Supported: 58 local food businesses were supported through technical assistance, business training, and seed funding, helping to build capacity within the local food economy. Residents Trained: 818 residents received hands-on education and training on topics related to local food systems like gardening, composting, and starting a food business. Partnerships Developed: 152 direct partnerships were developed with non-profit organizations, cooperatives, benefit corporations, and community groups and 116 indirect partnerships were developed through entities managing city-funded programs. 

 

In Fall 2024, the TruLocal Container Solar Vertical Farm Project was initiated through a partnership between the City (Office of Environmental Programs, Fire Department, Human Services Department), the Salt River Project, Arizona State University, and Homer Farms. The farm located within a food desert will be operational in mid-2025 using photogoltaics for energy efficiency combined with the innate water efficiency of vertical farming will be an example of a resilient, sustainable project. The community will also benefit from workshops available on vertical farming and twenty percent (20%) of the produce will be donated directly to the community. 

The Arizona Fresh Agri-food Innovation Center located on a former landfill site adjacent to the Rio Salado/Salt River within the South Phoenix area will begin construction in 2025 on the first of four phases of the project. The project will promote capital investment, job creation, and planning for entrepreneurial spaces for food innovation. A community park will also be developed on the site, along with green space along the Rio Salado. This project will be the largest Brownfields to Healthfields project in Arizona and provides increased access to healthy food and greenspace for the community along with research space for agri-food tech and urban agriculture innovation. 

The City established the Food Systems Program in the Office of Environmental Programs with general funds available for full-time staff and programmatic activities. Programs continuing from the RFSI, include the GardenPHX program (indoor and outdoor gardens for residents), Food System Transformation Grants, and Project REDUCE, focused on preventing and reducing food waste in restaurants. The City is developing the 2030 Food Action Plan with extensive community engagement including visioning workshops with residents, food system businesses, and nonprofits. The final plan is expected to be completed by the end of December 2025.

column16: In alignment with Phoenix's Climate Action Plan (CAP), the Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport identified the following CAP targets to serve as interim milestones to achieve the long-term net zero carbon goal: reduce carbon emissions from city operations by 40% by 2025 compared to 2005; achieve carbon-free electricity by 2030; and increase the efficiency of buildings by 30% by 2030 compared to 2012. Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport in Arizona has received the Level 4 'Transformation' Airport Carbon Accreditation (ACA) rating from Airports Council International - North America (ACI-NA) for the reporting year of 2021.To meet the Level 4 requirements, Phoenix Sky Harbor set itself the goal of achieving net zero carbon by 2040 for emissions (https://www.skyharbor.com/media/gy5hyr0e/aviation_department_roadmap_to_net_zero_carbon_external.pdf). The airport continues to pursue and maintain its carbon accreditation and in 2025, the Aviation Department has applied for Level 3 accreditation of the Goodyear and Deer Valley airports, furthering its commitment to track and reduce carbon emissions. Since 2014, Phoenix Sky Harbor has reduced annual carbon emissions by 42% through energy conservation measures and on-site renewable energy, despite growth and expansion. Some examples include reducing water usage by more than 24 million gallons a year, even with an increase in passengers served; reducing energy usage by 7% and focusing on solar power by adding panels at the Rental Car Center and East Economy Parking, Aviation HQ building and most recently at the airport's Command Center. Additionally, the airport has increased its waste diversion rates by more than 40% and has implemented waste diversion strategies, such as collecting food waste for composting and recycling asphalt and concrete into new pavements. Alongside this recognition, the airport also published a report, A Roadmap to Net Zero Carbon, on its plan to reach net zero carbon emissions by 2040. To achieve net zero carbon, Phoenix Sky Harbor Airport seeks to reduce 90% of 2010 carbon emissions, roughly 47,000 metric tons of carbon emissions remaining, before pursuing carbon removal technologies to account for residual emissions. According to the airport, the roadmap identifies the short-, medium- and long-term strategies for Phoenix Sky Harbor to reach this goal and satisfies the ACA requirement for identifying the specific carbon emissions reduction trajectory. A 210-kilowatt (kW) solar array was constructed at the Sky Harbor International Airport Emergency Operations Center and came online in April, 2024. The solar array provides about 55% of the center's electricity usage, bringing the total onsite solar capability to 5.2 megawatt (MW). The Phoenix Aviation Department has established plans to install additional solar photovoltaic systems at Sky Harbor International Airport to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040. The Aviation Department currently has four solar arrays installed, which provide 6% of the Aviation Department's total electric usage with renewable electricity. Seven additional onsite solar covered parking arrays are planned involving all three airports to maximize solar arrays across Aviation's facilities. The City's Aviation Department requires all new and renovated aviation facilities to be designed and built to Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) or Envision rating standards. LEED and Envision prioritize energy-efficient design. Envision is a sustainability and resilience indicator framework used to evaluate and quantify infrastructure project sustainability. Aviation has incorporated LEED standards into construction for several years, including the Terminal 3 modernization, which achieved LEED Silver in 2021 and the eighth concourse of Terminal 4, which opened to the public in June 2022 and achieved LEED Silver in 2024. Sky Harbor International Airport's PHX Sky Train Phase 2, which opened to the public in December 2022, was the first project in the Phoenix airport system that followed Envision standards, achieving Envision Gold in April 2020. The PHX Sky Train connects the 44th Street light rail stop, airport terminals, and the Rental Car Center. The two new PHX Sky Train stations are located at the Rental Car Center and the 24th Street Express Pay Parking lot. Completing the PHX Sky Train allowed the retirement of 78 compressed natural gas-fueled buses that provided shuttle services between airport terminals and the Rental Car Center.

column16: The City of Phoenix has a waste management strategy to divert 50% of material from the landfill by 2030 and 100% by 2050 (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/sustainability/2050-sustainability-goals/2050-waste-goals.html). Phoenix processed 124,876 and 119,420 tons of residential recyclables in fiscal years 2022 and 2023, respectively. The 27th Ave. Materials Recovery Facility (MRF) underwent a four-year renovation that completely replaced all the old sorting equipment with more modern sorting technology. The new machinery will increase sorting accuracy and decrease material contamination, which makes the resulting bales of cardboard, paper, plastics, and aluminum more valuable to buyers who remanufacture the materials into new products.  Additionally, Phoenix processed 39,007 and 40,241 tons of organic waste, respectively, in fiscal years 2022 and 2023. The waste diversion rate was approximately 31% for both years. Green organic waste is diverted from landfills partially through the Phoenix Green Organics Residential Collection Program. There were 7,852 tons of green organic yard waste collected in fiscal year 2021 and 8,108 tons collected by the City in fiscal year 2022. Additional green organic waste diverted from the landfill is brought directly to the City's 27th Avenue and North Gateway Transfer Stations by residents, other City departments, and landscapers. The City began collecting food waste organics for processing into compost at Sky Harbor International Airport in October 2023 in partnership with airport vendors. The Phoenix Convention Center reestablished a sustainable composting program in 2022. Composting removes organic material from the waste stream, creates less methane from decomposition than if it went to a landfill, and reduces transportation GHG that would result if the material were taken to the landfill. Composting also saves landfill space and creates a functional product. Phoenix hosts major events like Superbowl LVII and the 2024 March Madness Final Four. The City works to recycle as much waste as possible to make the events more sustainable. The Phoenix Convention Center and the Public Works Department worked together on large-scale events like the Super Bowl LVII NFL Experience Fan Fusion in 2023 and the Final Four Fan Fest in 2024. The overall waste diversion rate during Super Bowl LVII City-held events was 92.6%, qualifying as zero-waste with over 100,000 attendees. The 2024 Final Four Fan Fest had a 94.2% waste diversion rate for City-held events, qualifying as a zero-waste event with 52,283 attendees.

column16: Multiple climate factors interact with Phoenix's desert environment. A large, growing population and finite water resources present challenges. Resource managers must balance these with additional climate variability to ensure city resilience and longevity. All residents are vulnerable to climate challenges, with intensified impacts on those facing additional stressors like unreliable access to shelter, food, or water. The city of Phoenix has established a goal to reduce its gallons of water consumed per person per day (GPCD) in the Phoenix service area to 155 GPCD by 2030. The water consumed as of 2024 is 151 GPCD (https://cmpr-dashboard-phoenix.hub.arcgis.com/pages/wsd). The city of Phoenix 2021 Water Resource Plan (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/waterservicessite/documents/2021%20city%20of%20phoenix%20water%20resource%20plan.pdf) shows that, for most foreseeable scenarios, Phoenix has sufficient water supplies for the next 50 years and beyond. These supplies will likely be stretched even further through planned conservation and infrastructure enhancements. The City's “Save Water Pledge” was made permanent in 2025, which underscores the City's commitment to sustainability and water resiliency in the face of ongoing drought and climate challenges (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/water-services-news/phoenix-mayor-kate-gallego-announces-continuation-of-the--save-w.html). Phoenix, in partnership with Arizona State University and Northern Arizona University, has developed the report “Greenhouse Gas Inventory of the City of Phoenix Water System” that describes the associated greenhouse gas emissions of the water system from upstream raw water activities - sourcing water from the Salt-Verde watershed via the Salt River Project (SRP) and the Colorado River via the Central Arizona Project (CAP) - to the downstream uses of treated effluent. This is the first inventory of its kind for Phoenix and includes results from 2011 to 2021. The report shows that as the electricity grid transitions to renewable sources of energy, the associated greenhouse gas emissions from the use of water have decreased by 22 percent as a result. The GHG emissions per capita per day of water production are calculated for the city of Phoenix water system over the 2011-2021 time period and are 0.13 kg CO2e per capita day for 2021. The amount of embedded carbon in water consumed as part of the Phoenix water system is 0.73 g CO2e per gallon of water. The 501(c)(3) New Venture Fund's (https://www.guidestar.org/profile/20-5806345) project \'BlueBank\' (https://thebluebank.org/) is supported by the Phoenix Water Services Department's collaboration. BlueCommons funds water conservation projects for Phoenix businesses at little to no interest. The City's Water Services Department offered non-residential and residential (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/water-services-news/3259.html) turf replacement incentive programs of $2 per square foot removed in 2024 and 2025. Phoenix is a member and sponsor of the Arizona Municipal Water Users Association, enabling regional collaboration on responsible water use in Arizona (AMWUA, https://www.amwua.org/). The AMWUA mission is: \'Advocates responsible water stewardship that supports economic prosperity and safeguards Arizona's water supplies for future generations.\' Phoenix is a member and sponsor of the Arizona Water Association (AZ Water, http://azwater.org/), promoting a skilled water workforce and sustainable water resource use. The AZ Water mission is: \'Advocate for Arizona's water through bold leadership, connecting professionals, providing education, and inspiring environmental stewardship.\' The City of Phoenix supports The Nature Conservancy's (TNC) \'Arizona's Forests Program\' through partnership with the United States Forest Service to improve watershed health. TNC's program supports the health of the watersheds that provide water to Phoenix residents. The City aims to mitigate risk factors in the Salt and Verde watersheds and provide water quality benefits for the Phoenix water supply. The Phoenix City Council renewed its partnership with the National Forest Foundation for Forest Restoration and Watershed Enhancement in 2024 with a $2 million investment over a decade (https://hoodline.com/2024/06/phoenix-city-council-approves-2-million-partnership-with-national-forest-foundation-to-protect-water-supply/).

The strategic transportation plan of Tel Aviv-Yafo marks a significant shift in the city's approach to urban mobility. It reorders priorities by placing pedestrians and sustainable transportation options at the top and private vehicles at the bottom. This paradigm shift guides all current and future transportation initiatives to create a more accessible, environmentally friendly, zero-emissions, and efficient urban landscape.

Key Actions and Milestones: 
1. Cycling Infrastructure
In 2021, the city launched a comprehensive Cycling Plan aimed at significantly expanding the bike lane network in Tel Aviv-Yafo, which currently consists of around 330 lanes across the city with a total length of approximately 180 km (as of November 2023), aims to reach a total length of about 250 km by 2030. 
 The plan focuses on the following areas:
Expanding Bike Lanes: The goal is to create a city-wide, connected network of bike lanes, making cycling a safer and more viable mode of transport for residents and visitors.
Improved Connectivity: Efforts have been made to integrate cycling infrastructure with public transport hubs, facilitating seamless transitions between different modes of travel.
Rider Safety: Investments in cyclist safety measures include better road markings, dedicated cycling paths, and physical barriers where necessary.
Education and Awareness: The city has implemented educational campaigns to promote cycling as a sustainable option and address safety guidelines for cyclists and pedestrians.

Metropan is a bicycle and electric bicycle rental service with about 800 pairs of regular bicycles and 700 pairs of electric bicycles scattered in about 180 stations in the city.

Weekend Public Transportation - 'Na'im B'sofash'
Recognizing the need for accessible transport during weekends, when regular public transportation does not operate, Tel Aviv-Yafo expanded its Na'im B'sofash program. This initiative provides free public transportation services on weekends, linking Tel Aviv with key areas in the Gush Dan region. The service has become a crucial component in reducing reliance on private vehicles and promoting equitable access to transport.

Light Rail Development
The opening of the first light rail line in 2023 was a major advancement in Tel Aviv's transport network. This transformative project is part of a broader mass transit strategy to provide efficient, low-emission public transportation across the metropolitan area. The light rail is expected to reduce traffic congestion, improve air quality, and enhance mobility options.

Parking Standards - 
In alignment with its strategic goals, the municipality has updated parking standards to discourage using private cars. Starting in January 2025, The number of parking permits per household will be limited to two. City residents must pay for parking on streets outside their residential area. Parking rates in the Ahuzot HaHof parking lots will increase by 25%. 

Pedestrian-Friendly Zones
As part of the city's commitment to enhancing walkability, several streets have been closed to vehicular traffic and transformed into pedestrian-priority zones. These areas promote walking as the primary mode of transportation, fostering a more vibrant urban environment while improving air quality and reducing noise pollution. In the past two years, 25 streets have been converted into pedestrian-friendly zones.

A Prefeitura de Salvador tem como objetivo posicionar a cidade como uma referência nacional em construções sustentáveis. Essa estratégia visa reduzir inundações e ilhas de calor urbanas, promover o uso eficiente dos recursos naturais, valorizar a paisagem urbana e arquitetônica, além de contribuir para o embelezamento da cidade e o fortalecimento do turismo.
Com o apoio da GIZ (Agência Alemã de Cooperação Internacional), estão sendo conduzidos estudos técnicos e oficinas sobre Infraestrutura Verde e Adaptação Baseada em Ecossistemas (AbE) para Edificações. Como um dos resultados dessas iniciativas, foi lançado em junho o “Caderno sobre Infraestrutura Verde e AbE para Edificações”, com a participação de representantes da academia e do setor privado. O documento tem como objetivo oferecer aos atores públicos e privados uma introdução às práticas sustentáveis no desenvolvimento urbano, apresentando orientações práticas e exemplos aplicados. Ele também aborda temas da agenda climática internacional, oferecendo uma visão abrangente sobre o planejamento de soluções verdes e baseadas na natureza para as edificações.
Outra ação importante é o Programa IPTU Verde, que concede descontos no valor do IPTU para empreendimentos que adotem medidas voltadas à proteção, preservação e recuperação ambiental, minimizando os impactos da urbanização. Em 2022, o programa passou por uma revisão com o objetivo de incorporar novas práticas sustentáveis e critérios alinhados à agenda climática e às soluções baseadas em ecossistemas. A atualização também ampliou o foco para empreendimentos já existentes, que desejem adotar melhorias sustentáveis por meio de Retrofit Verde, com pontuação diferenciada em alguns requisitos.
Adicionalmente, a Prefeitura está desenvolvendo um projeto-piloto de Teto Verde de baixo custo, com potencial de replicação em larga escala. Paralelamente, está sendo estruturada uma rede de conhecimento sobre Tetos Verdes, envolvendo pesquisadores, arquitetos e profissionais da construção civil, com o objetivo de fomentar a adoção dessa prática em Salvador.
Como marco legal, em maio de 2024, a Prefeitura encaminhou à Câmara Municipal o Projeto de Lei sobre AbE em Obras Públicas, reforçando o compromisso institucional com uma infraestrutura urbana resiliente e integrada à natureza.

Salvador conta com o Plano de Mobilidade Urbana Sustentável (PlanMob), instrumento estratégico que orienta as políticas públicas de mobilidade para os próximos 32 anos, com horizonte até 2049. O plano está alinhado à Lei Federal da Mobilidade Urbana, à Política Nacional de Mobilidade Urbana (PNMU), ao Plano Diretor de Desenvolvimento Urbano (PDDU - 2016) e às Leis de Ordenamento do Uso e Ocupação do Solo (LOUOS - 2016).
O PlanMob contempla diretrizes e ações específicas voltadas à mobilidade urbana, considerando desde a macroacessibilidade, como a estrutura viária principal e os sistemas de transporte coletivo, até aspectos de microacessibilidade, que incluem a mobilidade de pedestres e ciclistas, calçadas, travessias e acessibilidade universal.
Entre os temas abordados estão:
- circulação viária,
- segurança no trânsito,
- integração entre transporte público e uso do solo,
- incentivo à mobilidade ativa,
- reestruturação institucional do setor de transporte.
O plano tem como principal objetivo melhorar a qualidade de vida da população soteropolitana e impulsionar o desenvolvimento urbano sustentável, pautado nos princípios de acessibilidade, segurança, eficiência, equidade e dinamismo econômico.

A Prefeitura de Salvador firmou uma parceria com a Humana Brasil para ampliar o alcance do projeto “Repense Reuse”, uma iniciativa voltada à economia circular têxtil. A proposta tem como objetivo estimular a reutilização e reciclagem de roupas, calçados, acessórios e roupas de cama, promovendo a redução do volume de resíduos enviados para os aterros sanitários e contribuindo para a mitigação das emissões de gases de efeito estufa.
Lançado inicialmente em 2021, Salvador foi a primeira cidade do país a instalar coletores públicos do projeto em espaços como parques e praças. Desde então, a iniciativa foi ampliada para diversos pontos estratégicos da cidade, como supermercados, escolas, shoppings, mercados e condomínios. Em 2024, já havia cerca de 168 coletores instalados em Salvador e na Região Metropolitana, localizados em bairros como Pituba, Itaigara, Stiep, Costa Azul e Candeal.
Os impactos ambientais e sociais da parceria têm sido expressivos. Apenas em 2024, estima-se que a iniciativa evitou a emissão de aproximadamente 2 mil toneladas de dióxido de carbono (CO₂) na Bahia. A cada 50 quilos de roupas reaproveitadas, deixam de ser emitidos cerca de 180 quilos de CO₂ e são economizados aproximadamente 300 mil litros de água, além da redução no uso de inseticidas e fertilizantes.
As roupas arrecadadas passam por um processo de triagem no centro operacional da Humana Brasil. As peças em boas condições são revendidas nas lojas sociais da organização, localizadas em bairros como Piedade, Itapuã e Uruguai, com preços acessíveis à população. Já os itens em pior estado são destinados à reciclagem e reaproveitamento por artesãos e costureiras locais. A renda obtida com a venda é utilizada para o financiamento de projetos sociais e comunitários, como cursos de capacitação em costura, hortas urbanas e outras ações voltadas à geração de emprego e renda.

A crucial aspect of the city's sustainability goals, as outlined in its community action plan, pertains to solid waste management. The city aims to achieve a “zero waste” status and plans to eliminate the disposal of solid waste in landfills by 2040. To accomplish this objective, Orlando has implemented several strategies, including the Residential Backyard Composter Program, a Weekly Recycling Collection Schedule, and recycling requirements for commercial and multifamily buildings.

One of the key components is the recycling ordinance, which requires owners of multifamily properties and commercial establishments to provide recycling services. While this ordinance is not specifically designed for construction and demolition (C&D) activities, it encompasses many renovation and tenant-improvement waste streams, fostering waste diversion practices throughout the city. This initiative directly contributes to reducing emissions generated by C&D activities.

It is also essential to note that the city is committed to adhering to LEED standards for its new city-funded buildings. This includes credits for C&D waste management as well as material and resources credits, which significantly enhance waste diversion efforts while promoting the use of lower-carbon materials in municipal projects.

Furthermore, the city has launched the Small Business Façade, Site Improvement, and Adaptive Reuse Policy (FSARP), which provides forgivable loans to facilitate the reuse of vacant or underutilized buildings. This policy supports the reduction of demolition activities and minimizes the embodied emissions associated with new construction by prolonging the lifespan of existing structures and salvaging more materials.

column16: OVERVIEW OF GOALS, OBJECTIVES AND TARGETS for Solid Waste from the community action plan: A reduction in waste will be achieved in part by expanding curbside recycling collection; composting; implementing innovative waste technologies; and providing educational outreach programs to the community. To achieve the zero waste goal, there must be a citywide effort to shift perceptions of the entire community on how a person's daily lifestyle of resource use and trash production have an impact on the entire community. Aside from the critical need to protect environmental resources and the well-being of Orlando residents, expanding support for local waste management businesses (such as commercial recycling and composting services) or pursuing advanced waste management techniques (such as anaerobic digester facilities that generate energy from both food waste and effluent) can also be economically beneficial, potentially creating new businesses and jobs. Furthermore, given the availability of nearby higher education institutions with research capabilities, the City of Orlando has the resources and research opportunities to explore innovative technologies and solutions to waste management. 2040 GOAL • Orlando strives to become a “zero waste” community and aims to eliminate sending solid waste to landfills by 2040. Additionally, municipal waste goals are outlined here, updated in 2017: https://www.orlando.gov/Our-Government/Departments-Offices/Executive-Offices/CAO/Sustainability-Resilience/2017-Municipal-Operations-Sustainability-Plan#section-8 . The city as a variety of existing programs or best practices identified in a 2023 assessment to execute on its strategy for zero waste. A few are described here: The Fix It, Don't Pitch It event is a free community event where community members may bring their common household items to be repaired by volunteers instead of sending them to the landfill. Electronics Recycling Events - This is a biannual event hosted by Keep Orlando Beautiful at Orlando Festival Park. Community members are able to drop off their unwanted electronics and textiles in a drive-thru. Accepted materials include computer monitors, televisions, telephones, office equipment, rechargeable batteries, electronic circuit boards and components, stereo equipment, clothes, shoes, home textiles, and stuffed toys. As of February 2020, the event has resulted in diversion of over 170,000 pounds of e-waste and textiles and 1,700 cars from the landfill. Curbside Recycling - Residents may participate in curbside recycling by placing all of their mixed recyclables including plastic, glass, paper and cans in their City-provided roll-off carts. The City's website includes helpful educational materials to inform residents of which items can and cannot be recycled and how they should be prepared for the bin (i.e., empty and cleaned with caps and lids on or off). The “Waste Wizard” item search feature allows residents to search for a particular item to determine if it can be recycled and where it should go. Commercial & Multi-Family Recycling - The City enacted a policy on April 1, 2019, revising the Solid Waste code to require all commercial and multifamily properties to provide the opportunity for recycling in phases over a four-year period. In order to demonstrate compliance with the policy, properties must provide a recycling container, implement a recycling program, and submit a recycling verification form to the city. The City's website includes educational resources for participants including information on the economic and business benefits of recycling. “What Goes Where” Online Tool - The City has established an online platform, where residents can view what items should be placed in a trash cart, recycling cart or composter. This program helps residents to understand what can be diverted from the landfill, and thereby has the potential to reduce contamination in the recycling stream. Single Use Plastic Bag, Straw And Foam Ban At City Events And Venues - This policy bans the sale and distribution of single-use polystyrene products on City property by City contractors or permittees and encourages the use of biodegradable, compostable, recyclable, and reusable materials.

The city has a set of strategies that are targeted at reducing the use of automobiles. These include Charlotte Bikes, Charlotte Walks, and the 2040 Transportation Action Plan. These strategies identify ways to facilitate the use of alternative means of transportation by increasing city-wide mobility. Consequently, they identify ways to make it safer to walk and cycle around the city, which has a positive effect on reducing carbon emissions by reducing automobile trips. The various plans that the city has developed to facilitate use of alternative modes of transit all support the concept of Transit Oriented Development (TOD). The intent is to create livable communities where people can get to the office, grocery store, restaurants, libraries, and parks without requiring the use of a car. The TOD approach makes provisions for providing extensive pedestrian systems throughout neighborhoods to minimize walking distance for residents and provisions for buffering cyclists from automobile activity with few conflict points. A significant example of this is the proposed Charlotte Gateway Station30 that will provide a multi-modal transportation facility that will merge public transit with intercity modes, increasing transportation options. Moreover, the project team also developed a Multi-modal Station Area Plan (MSAP) that identifies current priorities and transportation needs, like locating high density mixed-use development around the station. To further reduce transportation emissions, the Strategic Mobility Plan (SMP) works to offer everyone in our city safe and equitable mobility choices regardless of age, income, ability, race, and gender. This plan also supports the city's commitment to Vision Zero - eliminating traffic deaths and serious injuries - and establishing the 50-50 Mode Share.

column16: In June of 2018, the Charlotte City Council passed the Sustainable and Resilient Charlotte by 2050 Resolution, setting aggressive and aspirational goals for municipal and community-wide greenhouse gas emissions reductions. Specifically, it strives to have city fleet and facilities fueled by 100 percent zero-carbon sources by 2030. It also set a community-wide goal for Charlotte to become a low carbon city by 2050. The Strategic Energy Action Plan (SEAP), adopted by City Council in December of 2018, outlines how Charlotte will reach its goals by defining 11 linked action areas focused on transportation, buildings, energy generation, and workforce development/equity. The City of Charlotte recognizes that protecting our natural resources, promoting conservation, and improving the environment is fundamentally important to quality of life and essential to maintaining a vibrant economy. The City of Charlotte Aviation Department's Comprehensive Sustainability Plan reflects the Airport's commitment in helping the City achieve the objectives outlined in the SEAP. This plan includes the implementation of the Airport Carbon Accreditation which recognizes airport efforts to reduce and manage their carbon emissions. Charlotte Douglas International Airport has committed to the Level 1 Mapping of the Airport Carbon Accreditation by compiling a carbon footprint report and engaging an independent third-party to verify the report. This plan will enable us to become a leader in environmental stewardship by implementing best practices to help minimize the environmental impacts of our operations for the benefit of our local community. (5) Different Dinners. A trial to test what interventions would support willing Aucklanders to make food choices with lower impact on carbon emissions was successfully delivered. In October 2021, Auckland Council adopted the Sustainable Asset Policy. The policy, which aims to improve the sustainability of Auckland Council's Community Facilities, sets minimum requirements for sustainability ratings and carbon neutral operation for new buildings and infrastructure. Community Facilities has projects underway that the Sustainable Asset Policy applies to, these include: • The Scott Point Sustainable Sport Park development that achieved an Infrastructure Sustainability (IS) Leading Design Rating in 2021, the highest rating possible. The sports park is currently under construction and targeting a Leading as-built rating. • Te Whau Pathway, where the IS Essentials Rating tool is being piloted. This is a version of the IS rating tool that targets smaller infrastructure projects. A gold rating is being pursued and establishment works are underway for the first sections. • The Avondale Community Centre is currently being designed and is targeting a minimum 5 Green Star rating and net zero energy. • The Kaipātiki Eco Hub, which is under construction and is targeting a Zero Energy Certification under the Living Building Challenge. In addition to these projects in Community Facilities, for Auckland Council's new Albany Hub corporate office, the Corporate Property department is targeting a 6 Green Star interior rating. For the building itself, where Auckland Council is a tenant, 5 Green Star and 5 Star NABERSNZ ratings are being targeted. (2) Auckland City Library Green Roof. As part of the Central Library Roof Remediation Project, which aims to preserve the library building for years to come, Auckland Council chose to install a living roof that uses vegetation cover instead of conventional roofing. Living infrastructure has many environmental, economic, and social wellbeing benefits and helps us work towards Auckland's climate change goals. The project started in early July 2021 and was completed in April 2022. The roof's environmental and economic performance (energy efficiency, solar protection) will be monitored over the course of the next five years and results will inform similar projects. This is a sustainability innovation public housing pilot project by Kāinga Ora aimed at driving carbon emission reduction in New Zealand's construction industry. The project will deliver 30 new homes within five, three-level apartment buildings in Glendowie. Each near identical building will use a different construction technology, enabling sustainability insights to be gathered on a range of building materials and systems. Each building will achieve significantly reduced carbon and energy outputs; achieving both Passive House standard and net zero energy. (4) Sustainable urban planning.
